spots.name: Fort St. George
spots.label: Fort St. George

text.access_note: The fort is an active government complex, so some areas are closed and you may need photo ID at security, and the Fort Museum inside is ticketed; check the official site and any posted photography signs before you go.
text.geographic_location: Fort St. George stands on Chennai's coast. George Town grew out of the settlement that developed around the fort. The approach road is Rajaji Salai. Napier Bridge is a recommended additional spot.
text.description:
Fort St. George is where Chennai began. The English East India Company bought the coastal land in 1639 and finished the fort on 23 April 1644, St George's Day, which gave it its name. It was the first English fortress in India, and the city grew up around it. Today it is a working government complex. It holds the Tamil Nadu legislative assembly and secretariat, and the Fort Museum and St. Mary's Church are inside.

From outside, the fort photographs best as a classic exterior: thick walls about 6 metres high, the gateway and the colonial facade, all seen across the open approach from Rajaji Salai. The open space lets you step back and fit the whole frontage into one picture without cropping the edges. Inside the fort stands a teakwood flagstaff, 46 metres tall and one of the tallest in the country.

A phone does this subject well because the scene is mostly wide, even and architectural. Take one wide frame to show the whole fort, then move closer for details such as the gateway arch or the texture of the walls. Aim for morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the walls look warmer. If you have time, Napier Bridge is a recommended additional spot, with its white arches over the Cooum River.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Fort St. George area on Rajaji Salai, by taxi or hired scooter from wherever you are in Chennai. The phone icon on the map is about 3 minutes on foot from the fort, with the fort to the east of you. Walk east towards the walls and gateway. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the walls up with a horizontal grid line so the fort does not lean. Leave a little open ground in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Then take a closer shot of the gateway on its own. For a different view, Napier Bridge is a recommended additional spot, with its white arches over the Cooum River, and the waterfront and river banks alongside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. George's walls, in the entrance zone off Rajaji Salai. The fort lies to the east of you. From here you see the walls, the gateway and the colonial facade, framed against the open approach from Rajaji Salai.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot fit the walls in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gateway or wall details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the walls keep their colour. Avoid digital zoom beyond your phone's telephoto lens, as it softens the detail.

spots.name: Marina Beach
spots.label: Marina Beach

text.access_note: The beach is an open public space, but the lighthouse viewing gallery is a paid, ticketed lift ride, so check on the day for opening hours and fees.
text.geographic_location: Marina Beach runs along Chennai's Bay of Bengal shoreline, south of Fort St. George. The lighthouse viewpoint is near the southern end of the beach.
text.description: Marina Beach is a long, wide, sandy city beach on the Bay of Bengal, and it is where Chennai comes to stroll, fly kites and cool off in the evening. It is a natural beach that runs south from near Fort St. George, with an average width of about 300 m. That width is why it photographs so well: there is a lot of open sand and sea, with the city lined up behind it. The promenade was laid out in 1884 by the then governor, Mount Stuart Elphinstone Grant Duff, and statues and memorials were added along it over the years, including the Triumph of Labour and a Gandhi statue. It is one of the busiest beaches in the country, with around 30,000 visitors on a weekday and about 50,000 at weekends and on holidays. Swimming is legally prohibited because of the strong undercurrent, so photograph from the sand or the promenade rather than the water. The best overall picture comes from the Chennai Lighthouse observation gallery, near the south end of the beach. Time at the top is short, so have your phone ready and your framing in mind before you step out. If the lighthouse is closed or crowded, go down to the sand and shoot back towards the lighthouse, which suits a sunrise scene with the sea in front.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Chennai Lighthouse, near the south end of Marina Beach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the shoreline up with one of the horizontal lines so the curve of the beach leads the eye away from you. Leave about a third of the frame for sky and sea. For a different view, go down to Marina Beach itself and shoot a wide sunrise scene with the lighthouse behind and the Bay of Bengal in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Some visitors recommend sunset or evening, and others note that morning gives the clearest views. The beach is busier at weekends and on holidays, so a weekday morning is the quieter option.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Chennai Lighthouse (observation gallery near the south end of Marina Beach). A panoramic view from the top of the Marina, showing the whole length of the beach, the Bay of Bengal and the city skyline. From there the photo shows the whole length of the beach, the Bay of Bengal and the city skyline. The beach spot on the map lies to the north of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole beach, sea and skyline from the deck. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the shoreline. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out groups of people, kites or the statues on the promenade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Time at the top is short, so open the camera and turn on gridlines before you step out. Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sea and clouds keep their colour. Try a panorama along the shoreline, holding the phone steady and moving slowly.

spots.name: Government Museum, Chennai
spots.label: Government Museum

text.access_note: The view from Pantheon Road is public, but the museum complex and the Museum Theatre are ticketed, and photography rules inside vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the Government Museum Complex on Pantheon Road in Egmore, central Chennai. It shares the complex with the Connemara Public Library and the National Art Gallery.
text.description:
The Government Museum in Egmore is a colonial-era museum complex that can be photographed from the public road. It started in 1851, making it the second oldest museum in India, and it moved to its present site on Pantheon Road in 1854. The complex covers around 16 acres, with six buildings and 46 galleries. It also holds the Connemara Public Library and the National Art Gallery.

The simplest picture is taken from the public road, with no ticket needed. From there you can frame the old museum building and its facade from outside the complex. The middle of the complex lies a short walk to the north-west of that spot.

Inside the gates, the Museum Theatre is the other building to know about. It is a rare Italianate-style structure, built in the late 19th century. It has a high plinth, a tall flight of steps and a verandah of columns joined by rounded arches. You need an entry ticket to reach it, so treat it as an optional extra, or use it as a second viewpoint if you go in. Camera rules inside the museum can vary, so check the official site before you go. Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stonework.
text.directions_text: Navigate to Pantheon Road in Egmore and ask for the Government Museum. Get out at the main museum frontage on the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls do not lean. Leave a little sky above the roofline and keep your phone level. If you go inside the ticketed complex, the Italianate Museum Theatre is a good alternative subject, with its steps and arched verandah.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pantheon Road (in front of the main museum frontage). The colonial-era museum building and its facade, framed from the public road outside the complex. In front of the main museum frontage. From here your phone shows the colonial-era museum building and its facade, framed from the public road outside the complex. The middle of the complex lies to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade as the eye sees it. If you are standing close to the frontage, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the building in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out architectural detail without stepping into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Check the lens is clean before you shoot.
